section_summary: This section is dominated by public, clerical, academic, missionary, and congressional protests against American exports of arms, aircraft, petroleum, iron, steel, scrap, and other war materials to Japan during the Sino-Japanese War. State Department replies repeatedly explain that the Neutrality Act could not be applied unless the President formally proclaimed a state of war, that it would then restrict trade with both China and Japan, and that existing law did not authorize embargoes on commodities such as oil or scrap iron. The section also contains cross-reference sheets on proposed international sanctions, petitions from church congregations, and vivid missionary testimony about Japanese bombing casualties at Hankow and Wuchang.

subfiles.title: Continuation of State Department reply explaining the Neutrality Act
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Continues an explanation of why the administration had not invoked the Neutrality Act against China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that a presidential proclamation recognizing a state of war would prohibit arms exports and long-term credits to both China and Japan, but that no such restrictions were legally available without the proclamation. It says the President judged invocation contrary to the broader interests of the United States. The reply also notes that the act covered only enumerated arms and reports export-license values for both belligerents.

subfiles.title: Frank M. Silsley to Cordell Hull urging an end to shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Urges the State Department to stop shipments of arms and war materials that allegedly sustain Japan's invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: Silsley argues that American arms and long-term credits make the United States morally complicit in Japanese aggression. Citing millions of Chinese refugees, he appeals to national idealism and Christian duty rather than commercial profit.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Frank M. Silsley
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the legal and policy reasons for not applying the Neutrality Act to the Sino-Japanese conflict.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that the act would bar exports and long-term credits to both China and Japan only after a presidential finding that war existed. He says the President had decided that invocation was not in the country's practical interest and that the act did not cover ordinary commodities. The reply encloses the Joint Resolution and an arms-traffic pamphlet and supplies export-license totals.

subfiles.title: Frederick B. Stewart transmits a church resolution
subfiles.about: Transmits a unanimously approved letter from the Washington Park Methodist Episcopal Church Quarterly Conference.
subfiles.summary: Stewart reports that the church conference directed its secretary to forward the enclosed appeal to the Secretary of State. The accompanying resolution concerns American support for the Far Eastern war.

subfiles.title: Washington Park Methodist Episcopal Church appeal against war-sustaining trade
subfiles.from: Secretary, Washington Park Methodist Episcopal Church Quarterly Conference
subfiles.about: Calls upon Hull to end American trade sustaining the war against China.
subfiles.summary: The church conference describes the United States as becoming a partner in the Far Eastern conflict through war-sustaining traffic. It asks Hull to act against trade contributing to the destruction of Chinese lives and property.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Frederick B. Stewart
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to the Washington Park church appeal with the Department's standard Neutrality Act explanation.
subfiles.summary: The reply explains that an arms embargo would apply to both China and Japan only following a presidential war proclamation. It says the President did not consider invocation in the national interest and that non-arms commodities could not be prohibited under the act. Export-license figures and enclosures are provided.

subfiles.title: D. Brewer Eddy protests exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Protests American exports of munitions, gasoline, steel, and iron products to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Eddy endorses the pamphlet “America's Share in Japan's War Guilt” and calls American trade with Japan a moral failure. He reports strong public support at his speaking engagements for a firmer administration policy limiting such exports.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to D. Brewer Eddy
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains why the government could not prohibit arms or strategic-material exports to Japan under existing law.
subfiles.summary: Yost repeats that the Neutrality Act required a presidential proclamation and would operate against both belligerents. He emphasizes that gasoline, steel, and iron were not included in the statutory arms list or earlier international definitions. The reply concludes that no statutory authority allowed the President to prohibit those commodities and gives licensed-arms-export totals.

subfiles.title: Evarts G. Loomis protests a Japanese freighter's cargo
subfiles.about: Reports seeing a Japanese ship loaded at Brooklyn with aircraft motors, trucks, steel, and alleged shrapnel and demands immediate action.
subfiles.summary: Loomis condemns Americans for supplying a large share of the equipment used in Japan's war in China. He characterizes the profits as morally tainted and asks the government to remove the resulting stain on the United States.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Evarts G. Loomis
subfiles.about: Answers Loomis's protest by outlining the limits of the Neutrality Act and the administration's opposition to civilian bombing.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that an embargo required a presidential proclamation and would cover both China and Japan, while ordinary commodities remained outside the act. He cites arms-export-license totals for each country. The reply adds that the government had publicly condemned bombing civilians and had communicated that position to American aircraft manufacturers and exporters.

subfiles.title: Homer H. Dubs urges termination of military trade with Japan
subfiles.about: Urges the United States to stop supplying Japan with goods usable for military purposes.
subfiles.summary: Dubs expresses shame that the United States was assisting Japan despite broad public condemnation of Japanese conduct. He argues that the trade earned Japanese contempt and weakened American prestige in the Far East.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Homer H. Dubs
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Provides the Department's standard response concerning the Neutrality Act and arms exports.
subfiles.summary: The Department says it lacked authority to single out Japan unless the President formally found a state of war, in which case the embargo would cover China as well. It says invocation had been judged contrary to broad American interests and that non-arms commodities were beyond the act. Licensed-export figures are included.

subfiles.title: Brownell Gage praises Hull and requests action against exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Praises Hull's denunciation of aggressive force and asks him to prevent American participation in Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: Gage cites Hull's June 3 Nashville address condemning brutal aggression. He asks that the administration prevent sales of munitions and raw materials from making the United States a partner in Japan's war in China.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Brownell Gage
subfiles.about: Thanks Gage for supporting Hull's speeches and explains why the Neutrality Act had not been invoked.
subfiles.summary: The reply welcomes Gage's support but reiterates that a presidential war finding would impose an embargo on both China and Japan. It says the President had judged invocation inconsistent with American interests and that the act could not regulate commodities beyond the enumerated arms list. Export-license figures and reference materials are supplied.

subfiles.title: James M. Yard renews request to apply the Neutrality Law
subfiles.about: Argues that the Neutrality Law should be applied despite its effect on both China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yard acknowledges technical difficulties and the fact that more American war materials had gone to China than Japan. Nevertheless, he considers Japan the aggressor, questions the pretense that no war existed, and states that Chinese officials would welcome application of the law.

subfiles.title: Augustine Lonergan forwards Mrs. Parsons's protest
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent's letter urging an end to war-supply exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Senator Lonergan refers Mrs. Edgerton Parsons's letter to the Department for appropriate attention. He notes that he retained a copy for his files.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Edgerton Parsons urges an embargo on Japan
subfiles.about: Endorses action to halt American munitions and war supplies to Japan while its invasion of China continues.
subfiles.summary: Parsons briefly states her support for both governmental and popular action against exports to Japan. She asks Senator Lonergan to help secure such action for the duration of the invasion.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Mrs. Edgerton Parsons
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to Parsons's embargo request with a legal explanation and a statement condemning civilian bombing.
subfiles.summary: Green states that a Neutrality Act embargo required a presidential war proclamation and would apply equally to China and Japan. He says broader commodities could not be prohibited under the statute and reports licensed arms exports to both countries. The reply also describes the government's representations to aircraft manufacturers against materially encouraging attacks on civilians.

subfiles.title: Sumner Welles replies to Senator Lonergan
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Lonergan's referral and encloses the Department's response to Mrs. Parsons.
subfiles.summary: Welles confirms receipt of the senator's letter and the enclosed constituent protest. He supplies Lonergan with a copy of the reply being sent to Mrs. Parsons.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Irwin H. Linton report
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to a report from a U.S. missionary in China about Japanese atrocities and arms sales.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references an Irwin H. Linton document filed elsewhere. That report described Japanese atrocities and recommended discontinuing sales of arms and munitions to Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Koo's Geneva embargo speech
subfiles.about: References a telegram reporting Koo's League Assembly speech recommending broad sanctions against Japan.
subfiles.summary: The referenced telegram reported that Koo called for an embargo on arms, munitions, aircraft, oil, essential raw materials, and financial credits. The recommendation was made in a speech before the Assembly at Geneva.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Chinese embargo proposal in the League's Third Committee
subfiles.about: References a telegram reporting a Chinese request for an embargo on military aircraft and oil exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The document-file note points to a telegram from the General Disarmament Conference. It records that the Chinese delegate urged the League of Nations' Third Committee to embargo military planes and oil destined for Japan.

subfiles.title: Charles L. McNary refers the Carpenters' protest
subfiles.about: Requests State Department comments on an Oregon couple's protest against munitions traffic to Japan.
subfiles.summary: McNary reports that Leonard B. Carpenter and his wife strongly opposed American munitions shipments to Japan. He says they believed the United States should stop aiding Japan's warfare against the Chinese and asks for the Department's views.

subfiles.title: Sumner Welles replies to Senator McNary
subfiles.about: Provides materials and suggested language for McNary's response to the Carpenters.
subfiles.summary: Welles suggests sending the Carpenters the Joint Resolution and the pamphlet “International Traffic in Arms.” The proposed explanation says a presidential proclamation would impose an arms embargo on both sides, while non-arms commodities lay outside the act. Welles separately explains that the President had decided invocation was not in the country's broader interest.

subfiles.title: Pasadena Presbyterian Church petition sent through William G. McAdoo
subfiles.from: Dr. Freeman and members of Pasadena Presbyterian Church
subfiles.to: William G. McAdoo, for the President
subfiles.about: Petitions the President to end American trade assisting Japan's destruction of China.
subfiles.summary: The petitioners condemn Japanese attacks on noncombatants and state that American aircraft and munitions aid the aggressor. Invoking the Good Neighbor policy, they ask the President to place moral standards above financial interests. Two additional pages contain numerous congregational signatures.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment to Dr. Freeman
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the McAdoo-transmitted petition and points Freeman to an earlier substantive reply.
subfiles.summary: At Senator McAdoo's request, Yost acknowledges receipt of the September 18 petition bearing congregational signatures. He refers Freeman to the Department's October 6 response concerning the same subject.

subfiles.title: Missionary-society resolution sent to President Roosevelt
subfiles.from: David J. Fant, for the Board of Managers
subfiles.about: Transmits a unanimous resolution demanding an end to American material support for Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: The resolution cites Japan's alleged violations of the Nine-Power Treaty and Kellogg Pact and condemns attacks on undefended Chinese cities. It expresses shame that American aircraft, bombs, shells, scrap iron, oil, trucks, and raw materials supported Japan. Representing more than 500 churches, the board asks Roosevelt to use every practical means to terminate the traffic.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to David J. Fant
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the missionary resolution and explains the administration's legal position on trade with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost thanks Fant for supplying the resolution and repeats that the Neutrality Act could operate only after a presidential war finding and then against both combatants. He says the President did not consider invocation in the national interest and that ordinary commodities were not covered. The reply also reports licensed arms exports and reiterates the government's condemnation of civilian bombing.

subfiles.title: William G. Owens argues against supplying Japan
subfiles.about: Uses his experience in Shanghai to argue that the United States should stop exports usable in Japan's war.
subfiles.summary: Owens recalls Japanese efforts to manufacture an incident near Shanghai and Japanese claims that conquering China would make Japan independent in munitions. He argues that supplying Japan with munitions, cotton, iron, and oil violated both moral obligations and American commercial interests. He warns that a conquered China could become another Manchukuo and strengthen Japan strategically.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to William G. Owens
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Answers Owens's objections with the Department's legal interpretation of the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: The reply says an embargo could follow only a presidential finding of war and would apply to both China and Japan. It states that invocation was judged contrary to American interests and that the statute did not authorize controls on other commodities. Export-license totals and copies of the Joint Resolution and pamphlet are provided.

subfiles.title: Lillian Picken appeals to Roosevelt from India
subfiles.about: Urges legislation prohibiting exports of arms and all war materials to Japan and other aggressor nations.
subfiles.summary: Picken writes as an American missionary in Asia and says American bombs were contributing to the slaughter of Chinese noncombatants, especially women and children. She invokes Roosevelt's moral authority as president and Christian and asks him to lead the nation in accepting whatever sacrifices an effective embargo required. She encloses a missionary nurse's account of bombing casualties.

subfiles.title: Gladys Stephenson's Hankow letter with Florence E. Schafer's circulation appeal
subfiles.to: Florence E. Schafer; friends and prospective protesters
subfiles.about: Describes bombing casualties around Hankow and Wuchang and asks Americans to protest sales of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Stephenson gives a graphic account of maternity patients, refugees, children, and other civilians killed or wounded by Japanese air raids near Hankow and Wuchang. She describes the hospital's emergency work, the fear of repeated raids, and evidence that bomb components came from the United States and Britain. In an August 24 note from Kolhapur, Schafer identifies Stephenson as an English nurse and urges recipients to press Washington until the United States ends its part in China's suffering.

subfiles.title: Instructions to the American Consular Officer at Bombay concerning Picken and Schafer
subfiles.to: American Consular Officer in charge, Bombay
subfiles.about: Directs the consular officer to answer the two missionaries using the Department's standard explanation and enclosures.
subfiles.summary: The Department forwards the Picken and Schafer correspondence and a copy of Stephenson's Hankow letter. It suggests explaining that the Neutrality Act required a presidential proclamation, would apply to both China and Japan, and had not been invoked because the President judged it contrary to American interests. The proposed response also gives arms-export figures and points to Hull's public condemnation of aerial attacks on civilians.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Sherrod protests exports of war materials to Japan
subfiles.about: Protests American exports, including oil, scrap iron, and steel, that could support Japan's war effort.
subfiles.summary: Although the OCR is severely damaged, the letter is identifiable from the subsequent reply as Mrs. Sherrod's protest over war-material exports to Japan. Surviving phrases refer to arms and munitions as well as oil, scrap iron, and steel and call for their restriction.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Mrs. Sherrod
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains that existing law did not authorize an embargo on oil, scrap iron, or steel.
subfiles.summary: The Department repeats that the Neutrality Act could be invoked only after a presidential war proclamation and would then restrict both China and Japan. It specifically notes that oil, scrap iron, and steel were not among the defined arms and implements of war. The reply concludes that no current statute permitted the President or Secretary of State to prohibit their export.

subfiles.title: Walter G. Hiltner denounces exports and European appeasement
subfiles.about: Calls for action against shipments to Japan and condemns the treatment of Czechoslovakia by European leaders.
subfiles.summary: Hiltner describes exports of munitions, manufacturing machinery, and raw materials to Japan as a national disgrace and urges Roosevelt to appeal directly to merchants and citizens. He also proposes withholding loans and refusing recognition of territories seized by Japan. The second page condemns British and French concessions to Germany at Czechoslovakia's expense and asks American representatives not to participate in the perceived betrayal.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment to Walter G. Hiltner
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Hiltner's letter and refers him to an earlier Department response.
subfiles.summary: Yost records receipt of Hiltner's further communication about the Far Eastern situation. He directs Hiltner to the October 1 reply to a previous letter on the same subject.

subfiles.title: Ann Arbor correspondent criticizes American neutrality
subfiles.about: Rejects the Department's defense of equal treatment for China and Japan and advocates boycotts of aggressor states.
subfiles.summary: The writer thanks Hull for a prior letter and the pamphlet “International Arms Traffic” but cites The Nation's editorial “Partnership with Japan” in rebuttal. The letter argues that equal supply to aggressor and victim is a morally indefensible form of neutrality. It calls for boycotting or quarantining Japan, Germany, and Italy and contends that government foreign policy did not reflect American public opinion.

subfiles.title: Maude Scritchfield protests a San Diego scrap-iron shipment
subfiles.about: Protests repeated scrap-iron exports from San Diego to Japan and encloses a report of a planned 4,000-ton shipment.
subfiles.summary: A San Diego Union clipping reports arrangements to ship 4,000 tons of scrap iron from Pier 1 to Osaka. Scritchfield states that many such cargoes had already left San Diego and asks the Department for immediate attention to the Federation of State Societies' protest.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Maude Scritchfield
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains that scrap iron was excluded from the Neutrality Act's restricted categories.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that the act authorized restrictions on defined arms, ammunition, and implements of war in specified conflicts. Because scrap iron and similar products were expressly outside those categories, no statute then empowered the President to prohibit their export. The reply encloses the Joint Resolution and an arms-traffic pamphlet.

subfiles.title: Mechanicsburg Woman's Christian Temperance Union protest
subfiles.from: Miss Ehleman, for the Woman's Christian Temperance Union of Mechanicsburg
subfiles.about: Reports a unanimous resolution protesting American provision of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The union claims that the United States supplied half of Japan's raw war materials. It frames the issue as a Christian moral question and invokes the commandment against killing.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Miss Ehleman
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to the Mechanicsburg union's resolution with the standard Neutrality Act explanation.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that a presidential finding of war would trigger an embargo against both China and Japan, while no authority existed to discriminate against Japan alone. He says the President had judged invocation contrary to the broader national interest and that non-arms commodities could not be prohibited. The reply supplies licensed-export totals and encloses the Joint Resolution and pamphlet.

subfiles.title: Pasadena Presbyterian Church petition addressed directly to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: Dr. Freeman and members of Pasadena Presbyterian Church
subfiles.about: Petitions for an end to American sales assisting Japanese attacks on Chinese noncombatants.
subfiles.summary: This version of the Pasadena petition is addressed directly to Hull and repeats the charge that American aircraft and munitions supported Japan in an undeclared war. It asks the President to follow the Good Neighbor policy and place morality above profit. The following two pages contain the congregation's signatures.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Dr. Freeman
subfiles.about: Begins the formal reply to the Pasadena petition by explaining the conditions for invoking the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Freeman's September 18 petition and its numerous congregational signatures. It begins explaining that Section 1(a) required a presidential finding of war and that any resulting arms embargo would apply to both China and Japan. The reply continues beyond this section.
